property_summary: Only addresses marked admin can successfully create a new EmergencyOracle via newEmergencyOracle (i.e., calling newEmergencyOracle reverts for non-admins).
Only addresses that are admins cause newEmergencyOracle to succeed (i.e., the call reverts iff caller is not an admin).

Calling newEmergencyOracle should revert for callers that are not admins (i.e., reverted == true iff isAdmin[msg.sender] is false); the test asserts that if the call succeeds then the caller must be an admin according to C's public isAdmin mapping.
Calls to newEmergencyOracle revert for callers that are not admins (i.e., the call succeeds only when msg.sender is an admin).

For any admin caller, when newEmergencyOracle(description) is invoked the created EmergencyOracle.owner() equals the msg.sender passed to the factory (the admin); the mutant that passes address(this) instead will produce an oracle whose owner != msg.sender for some admin calls and thus violate this property.

For any admin caller who calls newEmergencyOracle(description), the newly deployed EmergencyOracle's owner() equals the caller (msg.sender); the mutant that constructs the oracle with address(this) breaks this because the oracle's owner becomes the factory contract instead of the caller for some admin callers.

For any admin caller A, when A calls newEmergencyOracle(description) the created EmergencyOracle's owner equals A (the factory forwards the caller as owner); the mutant that uses address(this) instead makes the new oracle owned by the factory (≠ A) for some admin caller inputs.

For any admin caller who invokes newEmergencyOracle(description), the emitted NewEmergencyOracle event's previous owner argument (first indexed field) equals the tx.origin (the external admin caller); the mutant that constructs the EmergencyOracle with address(this) (the factory) does not change the emitted event but does change actual oracle ownership — however, we instead assert that the factory's recorded isAdmin mapping still indicates the caller remains admin after creation (reference preserves msg.sender admin status), while the mutant also preserves it — that wouldn't fail. Instead, assert that the created oracle's owner() equals the factory's recorded owner via calling owner() on the new oracle contract immediately after creation; the reference sets owner to msg.sender (the admin) whereas the mutant sets it to address(this), so for some admin callers these differ and the mutant breaks.

For any admin caller A who invokes newEmergencyOracle(description), the newly deployed EmergencyOracle's owner() equals A (the factory forwards the caller as owner); the mutant that passes address(this) instead makes the new oracle owned by the factory, violating this rule for some admin callers.

For any admin caller and description, the newly created EmergencyOracle's owner equals the address passed into its constructor (the admin who should be owner); the mutant breaks this by calling transferOwnership after construction which can change the stored owner when constructor and caller differ.

For any admin caller and description, the newly created EmergencyOracle's owner equals the address passed as the constructor owner argument (the admin); the mutant violates this by calling transferOwnership after construction which can change the stored owner when constructor owner and msg.sender differ.

For every admin caller and description, the EmergencyOracle deployed by newEmergencyOracle has owner equal to the admin caller (the msg.sender of newEmergencyOracle); the mutant that calls transferOwnership on the freshly deployed oracle can change that owner when constructor owner and newEmergencyOracle's caller differ, breaking this invariant for some inputs.

For any admin caller and description, calling newEmergencyOracle should result in the created EmergencyOracle having its owner equal to the address stored in EmergencyOracle.owner() as set by its constructor (i.e., the constructor arg), while the mutant that invokes transferOwnership after construction can change that stored owner for some inputs (when constructor owner != msg.sender of newEmergencyOracle).

For any caller A that is an admin and any description, after calling newEmergencyOracle(description) the stored owner() of the created EmergencyOracle equals the constructor-passed owner argument (the first argument provided to the EmergencyOracle constructor); the mutant that invokes transferOwnership on the newly created oracle can change the stored owner when msg.sender of newEmergencyOracle differs from that constructor argument, so for some inputs the getter owner() will not equal the constructor argument.

For any admin caller A who invokes newEmergencyOracle(desc), the emitted NewEmergencyOracle event's first indexed argument equals the caller's address (msg.sender); the mutant emits address(this) instead and thus violates this property for calls where msg.sender != address(this).

When an admin calls newEmergencyOracle(description), the NewEmergencyOracle event's first indexed argument equals the caller's address (msg.sender) — the mutant emits address(this) instead, violating this rule for calls where msg.sender != address(this)).

For any admin caller that creates a new EmergencyOracle, the emitted NewEmergencyOracle event's first argument equals tx.origin (so when admin is an EOA tx.origin == msg.sender) — the mutant emitting address(this) can differ when the call is proxied through an intermediate contract, so using a proxy admin contract (msg.sender != tx.origin) will make the mutant break while the reference preserves the rule.

For any admin caller contract A (so msg.sender is a contract), when A calls newEmergencyOracle the CREATED oracle's constructor-recorded owner (readable via the emitted event's first parameter equivalent) should match A's address; the mutant emits address(this) (C) instead, so using a contract as the admin caller makes the mutant differ while the reference preserves that the caller-address (msg.sender) is the creator/owner recorded externally.

When any admin contract (not an EOA) calls newEmergencyOracle, the newly deployed EmergencyOracle.owner() (public getter) equals the immediate caller (msg.sender); the mutant does not change constructor owner but changes emitted event — however we assert that the returned EmergencyOracle.owner() equals the admin contract address after creation, which holds for reference for all inputs and will expose difference when the mutant's emitted event would have differed (we instead detect by creating admin contract that then reads the oracle owner via the oracle's owner getter to ensure it matches msg.sender).

For any caller address A, when A is marked isAdmin in the reference contract, calling newEmergencyOracle from A results in the created EmergencyOracle.owner() equaling A; the mutant that uses tx.origin can cause the created EmergencyOracle.owner() to equal a different EO A' (the origin) when calls are proxied, so the rule is violated for some inputs where a proxy is used.

For any caller address A that is marked as admin in the reference contract, if A directly calls newEmergencyOracle the created EmergencyOracle.owner() equals A; the mutant using tx.origin can be fooled when a proxy contract calls into C so the created EmergencyOracle.owner() is the proxy's tx.origin instead of the proxied admin, violating the rule for some inputs.

For any admin address A that calls newEmergencyOracle through an intermediate contract P (so msg.sender == P and tx.origin == A), the reference keeps the created EmergencyOracle.owner() equal to the immediate caller (msg.sender, i.e. the proxy P) whereas the mutant using tx.origin will set owner() to A; so the general rule: when a proxy (any deployed contract) that is itself an admin calls newEmergencyOracle, the created EmergencyOracle.owner() equals that proxy address — the mutant breaks this for some fuzzed proxy/origin addresses.

For every caller address A that is an admin (isAdmin[A] == true), when that address directly calls newEmergencyOracle(...) the created EmergencyOracle.owner() equals the immediate caller (msg.sender) — the tx.origin mutant can be made to create an oracle owned by a different address when the call is proxied, so it violates this rule for some inputs.

For any externally owned account caller A that is marked isAdmin in C, when A calls newEmergencyOracle directly (no intermediate contracts) the created EmergencyOracle's owner() equals A; the mutant using tx.origin can be made to violate this when a proxied call is used, so we instead assert that when an EOA admin calls directly the created oracle owner equals msg.sender — the reference satisfies this for all EOAs while the mutant can be broken via a proxy call from a different origin.
